## Reading this guide

This is the technical companion to the workflow guides. Start with
[Getting started](metrodag.html) to create a graph,
[Variables and analysis views](analysis-views.html) to annotate it, or
[Preparing figures for publication](publication.html) to choose output settings.
The sections below document the implementation and its constraints in detail.

## From a graph to a figure

Weakly connected components are laid out independently and packed by their
routed extents. Explicit user ranks retain alignment across components.
Route refinement caches unchanged obstacles and compares numeric unit-grid
keys, reducing repeated work without changing its acceptance criteria.

```{r causal-example, fig.cap="Publication defaults with explicitly supplied variable roles."}
library(metrodag)
g <- metrodag_examples("causal")
p <- metro_dag(g, exposure = "X", outcome = "Y", unobserved = "U")
p
```

```{r export, eval=FALSE}
save_metro_dag("dag.pdf", p)       # 180 mm wide; automatic height
save_metro_dag("dag.svg", p)       # vector artwork
save_metro_dag("dag.png", p)       # 600 dpi
```

Node names remain the graph identifiers. A named `labels` vector or the igraph
`label` attribute supplies readable display text. Roles are display annotations
provided by the analyst; plotting does not identify adjustment sets.

### Graph input compatibility

`metro_graph(nodes, edges)` constructs a graph from explicit node and edge
tables. `nodes$name` defines all variables, including isolates; `edges$from`
and `edges$to` must refer to those identifiers. Labels and explicit `role`
attributes are retained. `metro_graph_from_adjacency()` accepts a named dense
binary matrix: row A, column B equal to 1 means A -> B. Rows and columns can
be ordered independently. Direct two-column matrix inputs remain edge lists.

```{r table-input, eval=FALSE}
nodes <- data.frame(name = c("X", "Y", "I"),
  label = c("Exposure", "Outcome", "Additional variable"),
  role = c("exposure", "outcome", "observed"))
graph <- metro_graph(nodes, data.frame(from = "X", to = "Y"))
metro_dag(graph)
```

igraph subclasses from tidygraph and ggdag's `dagify()`/`tidy_dagitty()`
workflows are supported. ggdag is required only for its tidy objects; a plain
DAGitty graph retains its named labels without loading ggdag. The embedded
DAGitty graph defines the model and roles, while tidy-table labels take
precedence over matching graph labels. Inconsistent node/edge/status data is
rejected. Imports preserve identities, directed edges, labels and explicit
roles, then compute MetroDAG coordinates. DAGitty `[selected]` nodes import
with the `selected` role. Bidirected arcs are rejected unless
`bidirected = "latent"` draws each as an unlabelled unobserved common cause;
undirected and partially directed edges are not supported.

Check the chosen device size without writing a publication file:

```{r diagnose}
report <- diagnose_metro_dag(p, width = 180, device = "pdf")
report
```

`report$issues` identifies node, edge and label conflicts, with panel numbers
for comparisons. An error sets `report$ok` to FALSE; warnings still call for
visual inspection. Use the intended output format and fonts when diagnosing.
Overlapping station outlines are rejected during ordinary rendering, including
graphs without edges. Reversed ggplot position scales transform nodes and
routes together; nonlinear scales are not supported.

DAGitty selection nodes keep their role: they are drawn as double-outlined
squares, `highlight_paths()` conditions on them, and `check_metro_adjustment()`
refuses graphs with selection rather than ignoring it.

## Keep the graph fixed across analysis views

An adjustment set describes the analysis, while the DAG describes the assumed
causal relationships. Reuse one layout to show several analyses without moving
nodes, rerouting arrows, or removing unadjusted variables.

An omitted estimand label inherits from the layout when exposure and outcome
stay the same. A string replaces it and explicit NULL clears it. Changing the
exposure or outcome clears an omitted label.

```{r adjustment-views, fig.width=7, fig.height=5}
theory <- igraph::graph_from_edgelist(rbind(
  c("C", "X"), c("C", "Y"), c("X", "M"), c("M", "Y"), c("X", "Y")
), directed = TRUE)
fixed <- layout_metro_dag(theory, direction = "right")
crude <- metro_dag(fixed, exposure = "X", outcome = "Y", unadjusted = TRUE,
  estimand = "Unadjusted X-Y association")
adjusted <- metro_dag(fixed, exposure = "X", outcome = "Y", adjusted = "C",
  estimand = "Total effect of X on Y")
crude
adjusted
```

Squares mark adjusted variables; hollow circles mark observed variables not
adjusted for. Dashed circles still mean unobserved, which is a separate concept.
The legend and adjustment subtitle remain readable in monochrome. The input
graph and layout are not modified; each plot stores its selections in
`attr(p, "metrodag_analysis")`.

The estimand label is supplied by the analyst. Merely changing controls need not
change the target effect, and a mediator-adjusted model does not automatically
identify a direct effect. Plotting does not certify the sufficiency of a set or
mark open and blocked paths. The optional `check_metro_adjustment()` function
delegates total-effect checks to DAGitty separately. For a different
target on this same graph, for example the total effect of M on Y:

```{r another-target, eval=FALSE}
metro_dag(fixed, exposure = "M", outcome = "Y", adjusted = c("C", "X"),
  estimand = "Total effect of M on Y")
```

NULL role arguments inherit existing annotations. A supplied vector replaces
that role's previous set; `character(0)` clears it. `unadjusted = TRUE` clears
all inherited adjustment markers while retaining exposure, outcome and
unobserved status. Omit layout-computation arguments when reusing a layout.
Use `legend = FALSE` to suppress the legend or `ggplot2::labs()` to customize
the analysis title and subtitle.

Custom display categories are separate from these analysis annotations:

```{r node-groups, fig.width=7, fig.height=4.8}
grouped <- metro_dag(attr(p, "metrodag_layout"),
  node_groups = list("Background factors" = c("C", "S"),
    "Unmeasured influences" = "U"),
  node_group_colours = c("Background factors" = "#006D5B"))
grouped
```

Numbered marks stay inside the existing stations and identify categories in
every drawing style, including monochrome. Group numbers follow category names
in UTF-8 byte order. Outline colours are optional; analysis fills, adjustment
squares and unobserved dashes remain. Node identities, variable label text and
stored positions/routes do not change. Each node may belong to one group, irrespective of its
analysis role. Category names have no causal meaning and never infer selection
assumptions or adjustment recommendations; mark selection with `selected`.

NULL inherits groups from a reused layout; a new list replaces them and
`node_groups = list()` clears them. NULL colour overrides inherit matching
groups, while `node_group_colours = character(0)` clears only colour overrides.
These display annotations are stored in the layout's `node_groups` and
`node_group_colours`, separately from its `analysis` metadata. Legend text is
reflowed from the original category labels on each output device.

For a single figure with aligned panels and a shared legend:

```{r comparison, fig.width=7, fig.height=4}
compare_metro_dags(fixed, list(
  Unadjusted = list(exposure = "X", outcome = "Y", unadjusted = TRUE),
  Adjusted = list(exposure = "X", outcome = "Y", adjusted = "C",
    estimand = "Total effect of X on Y")
))
```

Every panel uses the same physical scale, including when titles differ in
length. Use `save_metro_dag()` to export the result at journal dimensions.
Nudge an individual label without changing geometry using, for example,
`label_nudge = list(C = c(0, 2))` to move it 2 mm upwards.
Supply `node_groups` and `node_group_colours` as shared comparison arguments,
rather than inside individual views. Every panel then keeps the same category
numbers and one combined legend.

With the optional DAGitty package installed, directed DAGitty DAGs can be passed
directly to `metro_dag()`. Isolates and exposure/outcome/adjusted/latent statuses
are retained. Other edge types are rejected explicitly.

```{r adjustment-check, eval=FALSE}
check_metro_adjustment(adjusted) # Valid total-effect adjustment for this DAG
check_metro_adjustment(crude)   # Invalid: C confounds X and Y
```

These checks concern graphical identification of a total effect by adjustment;
they do not validate the assumed graph, positivity or the statistical estimator.

## Layout algorithm

1. Validate a non-empty, simple directed acyclic graph and assign strict ranks.
   Longest-path layering initializes the default; supplied numeric ranks retain their
   order, including fractional ranks. Sink-aligned ranks are available through
   `layering = "sinks"`. The deprecated `"shortest"` option now uses sink-aligned
   ranks because shortest-path ranks are not generally monotone along edges.
2. Expand each long edge into private waypoints, one at each intermediate rank.
   Crossing reduction can now account for each occupied rank. Waypoints are
   excluded from the public node table and from the original graph.
3. Use alternating barycenter or median sweeps, retain the best crossing count,
   and perform local swaps that strictly improve it.
4. Align neighbouring ranks with isotonic compaction, preserving order and
   station separation. Choose each rank gap independently.
5. Route through the waypoints with vertical and 45-degree segments, penalising
   occupied tracks, intersections, and bends. Short edges are routed first,
   with deterministic ties. Leave shared sources early and approach shared sinks
   late to avoid crossing simple fans. This is a heuristic, not a global optimum.
6. Simplify complete arrows using straight, one-bend, and two-bend candidates.
   A candidate must improve conflicts, bends or length, avoid unrelated stations,
   and not increase crossings or shared track length. This removes avoidable staircases at
   waypoint boundaries; detours needed for a clear route are retained. The
   bounded candidate search does not claim a global minimum bend count.
7. Balance fans and their middle through-routes where station spacing permits.
   Accept more symmetric node positions only when crossings, pairwise shared
   track length, bends and total edge length do not increase and every route
   remains clear of unrelated stations.
8. Consider crossing arrows in pairs, keeping node positions fixed. A joint
   move must strictly reduce crossings without increasing pairwise shared track
   length or total edge length, and may add at most one bend. Routes must stay
   clear of unrelated stations. Try at most 24 crossing pairs (48 when `align`
   groups are given), with at most 24 shortlisted candidates per arrow, per
   component. This can escape a local dead end in which either arrow alone
   would overlap the other. The annotated U/C example
   has zero crossings and eight bends, versus one crossing and seven bends
   before this step. Outer bend alignment and the straight central chain remain.
9. Try to straighten the outer arrows of balanced fans.
   Align their endpoints and compact the gap, or move only the outer endpoints
   when compaction is blocked. Try at most 24 placements per component. Accept
   a placement only when total bends decrease, crossings, pairwise shared-track
   length and total line length do not increase, station spacing and clearance
   remain safe, and already straight arrows stay straight. All edges must retain
   their causal direction. With explicit user ranks a placement must keep
   every node in its rank, so only complete ranks move; alignment groups skip
   this placement step.
   The annotated example now has straight C-to-X and S-to-X arrows, four bends,
   and zero crossings. Its middle chain and aligned outer bends remain.
10. Simplify sections of remaining bent arrows while keeping their endpoints and
    all stations fixed. Short source/destination stubs and points near existing
    bends let a simple section replace a staircase even when the complete arrow
    still needs more than two bends. Accept only strictly fewer bends without
    increasing crossings, pairwise shared-track length or total line length,
    and retain clearance from unrelated stations: at least four grid units or
    the previous distance if smaller, with a floor of 0.8. Over at most two passes,
    attempt 24 routes per component, considering 24 sections and checking at
    most 128 shortlisted candidates per attempt. Explicit ranks are preserved.
    This is a bounded local search, not a guarantee of minimum bend count.
11. Compact gaps between whole ranks by removing the same number of vertical
    steps from every route spanning a gap. Preserve rank order and ties,
    including explicit ranks, four-unit station spacing, and existing route
    clearance up to four units with a 0.8-unit floor. Protect existing final
    approaches up to three steps. Try at most 24 candidates over two passes,
    accepting no increase in crossings, shared-track length, bends or length.
12. Lengthen final approaches shorter than three steps when an earlier run in
    the same direction can donate steps. This moves bends upstream without
    moving stations, adding bends or changing total length. Keep the same
    geometry and clearance safeguards; check at most 24 candidates per component.
    Some short approaches remain when neighbouring routes block the change.
13. Compact the transverse node arrangement. Connected straight arrows impose
    relative offsets when a rank gap shrinks. Move their components towards
    scaled or grid-aligned positions while preserving rank membership, ties,
    within-rank order and four-unit node spacing. Try at most eight feasible
    placements per component, with short-first and long-first routing orders.
    A route-step work budget reduces attempts for larger components and can skip
    this refinement entirely.
    Resize original route shapes and consider simple routes, then straighten
    and lengthen approaches. Accept only a smaller transverse extent with no
    increase in causal extent, crossings, shared-track length, bends or length.
    Already straight arrows stay straight; unrelated stations retain at least
    0.8 grid units of route clearance. Previous whitespace may shrink. After
    accepting a placement, repeat the bounded gap and approach refinements.
    Labels are placed later, so geometric improvement can still leave label warnings.
14. Reconsider automatic rank assignments. Move a node towards its neighbours
    when doing so reduces total incident rank span, or try equal-span moves for
    one-parent, one-child intermediates. Keep every edge strictly forward.
    Prioritize per-edge span savings, then lower degree and node name.
    Try at most three component rebuilds, further limited to
    floor(12,000 / (route steps × arrows)); larger components may skip this step.
    Trial ranks stay fixed during rebuilding, preventing recursive searches.
    Continue from accepted moves within the shared rebuild budget. Require
    smaller area without extra crossings or bends. A strict crossing reduction
    may spend 5% more total line length and 10% of either extent relative to the
    search input. Otherwise neither extent nor line length may grow. A longer
    shared diagonal requires strictly fewer crossings and no extra pairwise
    shared grid steps. Retain four-unit station spacing and 0.8-unit clearance.
    Individual routes, within-rank orders and metro path colours can change.
    Explicit ranks skip reassignment and retain their order and ties.
    This bounded search does not guarantee minimum area or label clearance.
15. For small components, compare child-directed coordinates and a
    reversed initial ordering with the established drawing. Rebuild each through
    the same pipeline, including rank refinement for automatic ranks, without
    recursively searching starting points; explicit ranks stay fixed in every
    start. Try at most two alternatives, further limited to
    floor(4,000 / (route steps × arrows)). Alignment groups,
    `ordering = "none"` and zero sweeps skip this search. Crossings and pairwise
    shared-track length cannot increase. Strictly fewer crossings can spend one
    bend per removed crossing (at most two overall), 5% extra line length and
    10% of either extent relative to the original drawing. At equal crossings,
    neither extent nor line length can grow. Up to two extra bends require at
    least 15% less area and a lower `bends + length / 20 + sqrt(area) / 4` score.
    Shared-length gains take priority within these guards. Require four-unit
    station spacing and 0.8-unit route clearance. The gallery's accepted variants
    reduce bends or length and area without worsening these metrics.
16. Relax source positions towards their children, using the child
    median and nearby transverse positions and, with automatic ranks, feasible
    later causal positions; explicit ranks admit transverse moves only.
    Reroute incident and newly obstructed arrows together. Compare at most 64
    candidates over four passes, further limited to floor(120,000 / (route steps
    × arrows)). Alignment groups, disabled ordering and zero sweeps skip
    this pass. Do not increase crossings, pairwise shared length, bends, line
    length or either extent. Preserve straight arrows, four-unit station spacing
    and 0.8-unit route clearance. Do not add transverse direction reversals,
    including in subsequent gap/arrangement compaction. Automatic source ranks
    and within-rank orders can change; the graph and analysis roles do not.
17. Place low-degree intermediates between their parents and children, within
    their rank when ranks are explicit.
    Protect collinear straight through-chains, or the straight arrow with the greatest causal span
    when no through-chain exists. An isolated side arrow may gain a bend while
    its neighbour straightens. Try at most 24 placements, further limited to
    floor(60,000 / (route steps × arrows)), and accept one best move. Alignment
    groups, disabled ordering and zero sweeps skip this pass. Evaluate
    final half-grid routes, requiring smaller area without more crossings,
    shared length, line length, either extent or any arrow's transverse reversals.
    One extra bend requires at least 15% less area, two at least 25%, and a lower
    score: area ratio + 0.5 × length ratio + 0.1 × extra bends. Crossings then
    shared length take priority within those guards. Preserve four-unit station
    spacing and 0.8-unit unrelated-station clearance. Automatic ranks and
    within-rank orders reflect the new geometry; labels and roles stay unchanged.
    Apply the same bounds to unit-grid routes, since the half-grid pass may skip
    a packed drawing under its work limit.
18. For automatic ranks, start again from other automatic layerings: the
    minimum-span layering, which moves each node to the end of its legal rank
    interval on the side with more arrows until the total rank span stops
    falling, and the other of the source- and sink-aligned layerings. Skip a
    layering whose rank order equals one already tried. Try at most two, further
    limited to floor(8,000 / (route steps × arrows)). Each trial runs steps
    2-13 and is screened against the best drawing before step 16 under the
    step 15 rule. The best trial then receives steps 14, 16 and 17, and is kept
    only when the step 15 rule still prefers it to the relaxed drawing from the
    requested layering: relaxation can recover the gain the screen saw. Bends,
    shared length and line length count from the relaxed drawing; a crossing
    reduction keeps its 10% extent allowance over the drawing the search
    started from, since relaxation compacts that drawing first.
    Explicit ranks/alignment, `ordering = "none"` and zero sweeps skip this step.
19. After placement and component packing, try the same routing grammars on a
    doubled integer grid, then rescale to half-unit steps. Stations, ranks,
    explicit alignment and straight arrows stay fixed. Accept a strict geometry
    improvement without more crossings, shared length, bends, line length,
    routed extent or transverse reversals on any arrow. Scale the required
    station clearance too: 1.6 on the doubled grid retains 0.8 layout units.
    Skip drawings with 2 × route steps × arrows > 400,000. Earlier passes route
    one arrow at a time, so a bending sibling can take the straight track between
    two stations on one line and push the arrow that joins them onto a parallel
    lane with a hook at each end, as in a five-mediator fan. The pass therefore
    also gives such arrows their straight track, reroutes (crossings first) the
    bending arrows that then share that track, and keeps that result when it
    meets the same guards with no more crossings or bends than the plain search.
    This attempt roughly doubles the pass, so it is made only up to
    2 × route steps × arrows = 250,000.
    Only geometrically
    changed arrows receive half-unit rows; unchanged arrows keep their rows.
    This pass runs after every earlier unit-grid search, including rank rebuilds.
20. Rotate the geometry to the requested direction. The stored geometry remains
   monotone and preserves every original edge and its endpoints.

Refinement and metro path-cover ties use node names, and path colour indices
follow the path-source name order. Reordering equivalent graph inputs therefore
retains default geometry and styling. `ordering = "none"` deliberately retains
the supplied vertex order. Explicit ranks can be named by node or supplied in
vertex order; only their ordering and ties determine layers, not numeric gaps.
Every node keeps its supplied rank. The gaps between layers and the order and
transverse positions within a layer remain free, so the placement refinements
above still run with moves restricted to those freedoms, while rank reassignment
is skipped.
Automatic layers, within-layer orders and gap metadata reflect the refined
positions. Source- and sink-aligned layering specify starting ranks rather than
fixed final positions; use explicit `rank` values when those ties must remain.

For repeated measures, `align = list(c("X1", "X2", "X3"))` explicitly names
stations that share a row in a horizontal drawing, or a column in a vertical
drawing. Supply `rank` separately for wave ordering. The algorithm never infers
repeated-variable identity or adjustment recommendations from names. Alignment
can add crossings, bends and space: in README DAG 6 it gives eight crossings
instead of five, and area 207 instead of 180, while keeping both repeated chains
straight. The separately rendered rank-only example makes that choice visible.

Station fan placement preserves one complete straight arrow's bearing when
possible. Displaced incoming attachments blend tangentially into their radial
arrow shafts if the final device-space strokes, heads, station outlines and
figure bounds remain clear. Otherwise the previous attachment is retained.
Tied bearings follow the first geometric divergence looking out from the station;
endpoint names break only geometric ties. A source port can join a nearby branch
after it diverges, rather than return to the shared track. Its cubic control
points must be monotone in the original bearing and outward transverse direction.
The join is limited to 12 mm of the original shaft and goes through the same
final ink-clearance checks. These attachment changes do not alter stored routes.
The stored grid routes and causal topology are unchanged by rendering.

`layout_metrics()` reports `shared_track_length` in layout units alongside
`overlap_segments`. The former sums each overlapping pair's actual shared
length, including partial overlaps; a track shared by three arrows contributes
three times its length. Device diagnostics remain necessary because labels,
station sizes and fanned attachments are added after geometry is measured.

Reused layouts are checked before plotting and computing `layout_metrics()`.
They must contain exactly one node row per graph vertex and one continuous
route per graph edge. Coordinates must be finite real numbers, with unique
numeric `segment` ordering values within each edge. Adjacent segments must
share endpoints exactly; the route must join the coordinates of its named
source and destination. Incomplete routes are rejected, so exports cannot
silently bridge a deleted step or reconnect a moved station. Row permutations
and opaque route IDs remain supported without modifying the stored tables.
Empty string IDs and distinct numeric IDs with identical printed forms remain
separate during metrics and attachment placement. `count_crossings()` counts
the places where one arrow passes to the other side of another, so arrows that
fork from or merge into a station, or share a section and leave it on the
sides they entered, are not crossings; the refinement passes above compare
contact points, which also count such forks. On a standalone segment table it
still permits gaps and compares a route with gaps piece by piece.
Redundant zero-length steps are ignored for drawing, attachment bearings and
straight-run overlap metrics. A route with no nonzero segment instead reports
an `edge_zero_length` error at draw time, identifying its source and destination.
Recompute such geometry or give its endpoints distinct positions; changing the
output size cannot make a collapsed route visible. Stored rows remain unchanged.

The regular grid and separated waypoints prevent a long route from running
through unrelated nodes. Shared tracks and crossings can remain in dense
examples. There is no hidden bundling or causal edge deletion.
The bounded joint search is an additional runtime cost and does not establish
that any remaining crossing is unavoidable.

## Rendering at the actual output size

The renderer uses millimetres on the active graphics device. It trims routes to
station rims and fans incident attachments apart where several edges approach
from the same direction. These short physical attachments need not be exactly
45 degrees; the stored layout remains octilinear. High-degree stations grow
slightly to accommodate the arrows. A straight final approach keeps each
arrowhead aligned with its shaft and directed toward the destination rim.

Labels are wrapped, including identifiers without spaces (after `_`, `.`,
`-` and `/`, and at camelCase boundaries),
measured with the selected font, and placed among compass
positions using node, route, label, and boundary collision costs. A label
also costs more when another arrow runs between it and its station, cutting
it off, and when it passes within 1.5 mm of a route without touching it;
farther rings cost more, so that clearance moves a label only a little.
`diagnose_metro_dag()` reports labels left cut off more than 7 mm from their
station as `label_association`.
Placement is
checked against the final trimmed routes, their stroke widths and filled
arrowheads, and recomputed on resizing and export. Some crowded figures cannot fit all labels;
warnings identify remaining collisions so the analyst can increase the output
size or abbreviate labels. Custom `fontface`, `lineheight`, and text `colour`
are supported; arbitrary `geom_text()` arguments are not used by this renderer.
Wrapping uses character limits and the available physical width; set
`label_wrap = NULL` to keep manual line breaks without automatic wrapping.
Joint pair reconsideration can free a station's nearby slot when another label
has occupied it. Up to 24 pair attempts over two passes compare 16 shortlisted
positions plus the current choice per label; sets above 32 nonempty labels skip
the pair search. Association costs discourage labels closer to another station.
If conflicts remain, up to two placements try physical reflows at 75% and 50%
of the original label width for up to six affected labels. Accept only fewer
conflicts without increasing any of station, route, label or boundary
obstructions. Words and intentional newlines are retained; unresolved conflicts
still produce diagnostics. These bounded searches do not guarantee clearance.
Within each original line, automatic wrapping moves a preceding word onto a
solitary numeric line when the pair fits. This keeps short word/number groups
together without changing words, exceeding the wrap width or overriding
intentional line breaks. It does not identify repeated variables.
Manual label nudges are applied afterwards and included in collision checks.
Placement respects the final theme's plot margins, including zero margins.
Titles, subtitles and captions are measured and wrapped on the drawing device,
including ordinary printing and `ggplot2::ggsave()`. If station and arrow
clearance would consume an edge or a route would overlap an unrelated station,
rendering stops and identifies the conflict. Attachments entering their own
source or destination station are also rejected. Arrowheads are drawn after
route casings to preserve their visibility at crossings. Route and station
outline widths use physical millimetres. Automatic export height follows the
displayed panel proportions, including fixed coordinate ratios, theme aspect
ratios and flipped comparison panels. `save_metro_dag()` preserves an
existing output file if rendering fails and accepts an existing output
directory through `path`.
Exporting a layout and failed comparison construction preserve ggplot2's
previous last plot. Comparisons accept `newpage` and `vp` during printing for
composition in grid viewports. Adjustment subtitles fall back to node
identifiers when a selected covariate's display label is blank.

The default publication style uses fine charcoal routes and a white background.
`style = "metro"` uses path-cover colours; `style = "monochrome"` keeps roles
usable without colour. Path colours have no automatic causal interpretation.

## Diagnostics and limitations

```{r causal-metrics}
layout_metrics(attr(p, "metrodag_layout"))
```

Metrics describe the stored geometry before device-dependent arrow attachments
and labels. A crossing is counted where one arrow passes from one side of
another to the other side (see `?count_crossings`). Arrows that fork from or
merge into a station, touch at a point, or share a section and leave it on the
sides they entered are not crossings; an arrow that runs through a shared
section and leaves on the other side crosses once. The refinement passes
still compare contact points between routes, which also count forks and
touches, so the two counts can differ on the same drawing. Overlaps are
counted after straight runs are merged. Node–edge collisions count unrelated
node/edge pairs less than half a grid unit apart.

These diagnostics support engineering checks. They do not establish perceptual
superiority, global optimality, or causal validity. Dense DAGs can have unavoidable
crossings and shared tracks; large graphs may need multiple figures. A controlled
readability study and broader algorithm comparison remain future work.
